Other factors to consider are comorbid condi- tions and potential drug interactions with associated medica- tions.1-4 Neoplastic disorders in the elderly have been undertreat- ed because of an impression that these diseases are less aggressive,5 and the effects of chemotherapy more likely to be severe.1,2,5,6 Elderly patients have often been excluded from clin- ical trials for reasons that included physician bias, protocol eligi- bility criteria with restrictions on comorbidities, and poor patient functional status.7 There is evidence, however, that healthy older patients can tolerate chemotherapy as well as younger patients.1,2 However, there have been few studies of chemotherapy specifi- cally in elderly patients,4,5 and selection of a suitable dosage reg- imen is more difficult as a consequence, although there is in- creasing effort to address this lack of data.2,5,6 Old people vary as much as any other group in their response to drugs, and the con- sensus is that they should not be excluded from any form of treat- ment on the grounds of age alone. 1. Outpatients taking oral antineo- plastic therapy at home do not receive the same level of monitor- ing as inpatients, and should be cautioned to report any adverse effects, since such treatments may still produce severe toxicity. Contraception. The BNF recommends that intra-uterine de- vices for contraception be used with caution in patients with drug- or disease-induced immunosuppression, because of the risk of infection; such devices are contra-indicated in marked im- munosuppression.
